title: The app that predicts lunch
paragraphs: A secondary school has begun using a simple prediction tool to estimate how many students will choose each cafeteria meal. The system uses past sales, the day of the week and whether special events are scheduled. Staff hope the forecasts will reduce food waste without leaving students with too few choices.

The first month produced mixed results. Predictions were accurate on ordinary days but failed badly during a week of unusually hot weather, when far fewer students chose the soup option. The software had no weather data because designers had not considered temperature important when building the first version.

Rather than calling the tool a failure, the school treated the mistake as information. Weather data was added, but staff also decided that the model should never determine quantities automatically. The cafeteria manager can adjust the recommendation if she knows about a class trip, a sports tournament or another event not yet recorded in the system.

Computer-science teacher Ravi Sen says this is the lesson he wants students to notice: prediction tools are built from selected information, so their limits often reveal what designers forgot to include. A useful model does not remove human judgment; it makes the basis of a decision clearer and gives people another source of evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the prediction tool?
options: To remove all cafeteria staff
To estimate meal demand and reduce waste
To choose what students are allowed to eat
To predict examination results
questions.explanationJa: meal demandを予測してfood wasteを減らすことが目的です。

questions.prompt: Give two types of information the original model used.
markscheme: Past meal sales and/or the day of the week.
questions.explanationJa: past sales、weekday、eventsなどです。

questions.prompt: True or false: The school stopped using the tool after the hot-weather error.
questions.justification: The school treated the error as useful information, added weather data and kept the tool with human adjustment.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。errorからmodelを改善しました。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 4 meaning 'chosen from a larger possible set'.
questions.explanationJa: selected＝選択された。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, what does 'the recommendation' refer to?
options: The meal quantities suggested by the prediction tool
The weather forecast
A student's food choice
The school timetable
questions.explanationJa: modelがsuggestするquantitiesです。

questions.prompt: Why does the school keep human adjustment in the system? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Staff may know about events or conditions not included in the model's data.
Human judgment can correct or interpret the model rather than letting an incomplete prediction control quantities automatically.
questions.explanationJa: model外のcontextとhuman judgmentの必要性です。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: A useful model does not remove human ________.
questions.explanationJa: human judgment が本文です。

questions.prompt: What is Sen's attitude toward prediction errors?
options: They prove prediction tools are useless.
They can reveal missing assumptions or data and help improve the model.
They should be hidden from students.
They matter only when money is lost.
questions.explanationJa: errorをmodel limitationを知るevidenceとして捉えています。

questions.prompt: What is the report's broader message about technology? Give two ideas.
markscheme: Digital models depend on the information and assumptions chosen by designers.
Technology can support decisions best when its limitations are visible and human judgment remains involved.
questions.explanationJa: data selectionとhuman oversightが中心です。

title: Should students use AI feedback?
paragraphs: Several teachers at Brookfield College are testing an AI tool that comments on early drafts of student writing. The tool does not assign grades. Instead, it highlights unclear sentences, repeated ideas and places where a claim may need evidence. Students can decide whether to accept any suggestion.

Supporters say immediate feedback can help students revise more often. A teacher may need several days to respond to thirty drafts, while software can provide a first reaction within seconds. However, teachers warn that fast feedback is not necessarily good feedback. The system sometimes recommends removing unusual wording that is perfectly understandable but less common in its training data.

To reduce this problem, students are required to label each suggestion they accept with a brief reason. They also choose one suggestion to reject and explain why. Teacher Maya Chen says this turns the tool from an answer machine into an object of evaluation: students must decide whether the advice actually improves meaning, evidence or style.

The trial will compare revision quality, not simply the number of changes made. Teachers are especially interested in whether students become more independent editors over time. If students accept every suggestion automatically, Chen says, the tool may make writing smoother while making judgment weaker.

questions.prompt: What does the AI tool do?
options: It gives final grades.
It provides comments on early drafts without making the final decision.
It writes complete essays automatically.
It replaces all teachers.
questions.explanationJa: draftへのfeedbackを出しますがgradingはしません。

questions.prompt: Give one advantage and one limitation of the tool mentioned in paragraph 2.
markscheme: Advantage: it can provide feedback very quickly and encourage more revision.
Limitation: it may incorrectly discourage unusual but valid wording or give advice shaped by training-data patterns.
questions.explanationJa: speedとquality/biasのtrade-offです。

questions.prompt: True or false: Students are expected to accept all AI suggestions.
questions.justification: Students must justify accepted suggestions and deliberately reject and explain at least one suggestion.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。evaluateしてrejectすることもtaskです。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 3 meaning 'careful judgment of quality or value'.
questions.explanationJa: evaluation＝評価。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, what does 'this problem' refer to?
options: The AI sometimes gives questionable advice, especially about uncommon wording
Teachers taking too long to grade final exams
Students refusing to write drafts
The lack of computers
questions.explanationJa: AI suggestionのquality problemを指します。

questions.prompt: Why must students explain accepted and rejected suggestions? Give two ideas.
markscheme: The explanation forces students to evaluate the advice rather than follow it automatically.
It helps students practise judging whether a change improves meaning, evidence or style.
questions.explanationJa: critical evaluationとeditorial judgmentを育てます。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Teachers want students to become more independent ________.
questions.explanationJa: independent editors が本文です。

questions.prompt: What is Chen's main concern?
options: Students may write too slowly.
Automatic acceptance could improve surface smoothness while weakening judgment.
AI feedback contains no language at all.
Teachers will have too much free time.
questions.explanationJa: smoothnessとjudgmentのtrade-offを心配しています。

questions.prompt: What is the article's overall position on AI feedback? Give two ideas.
markscheme: AI feedback can be useful for speed and revision when treated as advice rather than authority.
Its educational value depends on students evaluating suggestions and developing their own judgment.
questions.explanationJa: toolとしての有用性とcritical useの条件を示しています。

title: The tiny satellite club
paragraphs: At a school in Scotland, students are building a satellite small enough to fit inside a shoebox. The device will not travel into space during the school project. Instead, it will be lifted by a high-altitude balloon to collect temperature and pressure data before returning by parachute.

The club began because physics teacher Iain Ross wanted students to experience a complete engineering cycle. In normal lessons, experiments often end once a result has been recorded. The satellite project forces students to consider weight, battery life, weather, communication range and what happens if a component fails far from the launch site.

Students quickly discovered that adding more sensors did not automatically make the design better. Every extra device used power and increased weight. One team wanted a camera, but keeping it would have required a larger battery and reduced space for the main science instruments. They eventually removed the camera, even though it was the feature they found most exciting.

Ross says the most important lesson is that engineering involves choosing among competing good ideas. Success is not measured by how many features a device contains but by whether it performs its main purpose reliably within real constraints. The club plans to publish both successful data and design decisions that did not work as expected.

questions.prompt: How will the student satellite be tested?
options: It will orbit Earth for a year.
A high-altitude balloon will carry it to collect data before parachute return.
It will remain permanently in the classroom.
It will be launched from a rocket to the Moon.
questions.explanationJa: balloon testでtemperature/pressure dataを取ります。

questions.prompt: Give two engineering constraints students must consider.
markscheme: Weather, communication range and/or failure of components far from the launch site.
questions.explanationJa: weight、power、weather、rangeなどです。

questions.prompt: True or false: The students kept the camera because it was the most exciting feature.
questions.justification: They removed the camera because it required more battery power and reduced space for the main science instruments.
questions.explanationJa: Falseです。excitingでもmain purposeを優先して外しました。

questions.prompt: Find the word in paragraph 4 meaning 'dependably, with consistent success'.
questions.explanationJa: reliably＝確実に。

questions.prompt: In paragraph 3, what does 'keeping it' refer to?
options: Keeping the camera in the design
Keeping the balloon indoors
Keeping the project secret
Keeping every failed component
questions.explanationJa: cameraをdesignに残すことです。

questions.prompt: Why can adding more sensors make the satellite worse? Give two linked ideas.
markscheme: Extra sensors increase power use and/or weight.
They can reduce space or resources available for instruments essential to the main scientific purpose.
questions.explanationJa: more featuresがresource trade-offを生みます。

questions.prompt: Complete from paragraph 4: Engineering involves choosing among competing good ________.
questions.explanationJa: competing good ideas が本文です。

questions.prompt: What is Ross's view of engineering success?
options: A design is best when it has the most features.
Success means reliably achieving the main purpose within constraints.
Students should avoid difficult choices.
Only successful results should be published.
questions.explanationJa: feature countではなくpurpose/reliabilityを重視しています。

questions.prompt: Why is publishing unsuccessful design decisions educationally useful? Give two ideas.
markscheme: It shows how engineering decisions are revised when ideas fail or constraints become visible.
It makes the reasoning process and trade-offs available for others to learn from, not only the final successful data.
questions.explanationJa: failure processもengineering learningの一部として公開します。

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the feature?
options: To advertise commercial satellites
To show how a school engineering project teaches trade-offs, constraints and reliability
To argue cameras should never be used in science
To explain only atmospheric pressure
questions.explanationJa: engineering cycleとtrade-off learningが中心です。
